questions.stem: What does the principle of state sovereignty mean in international law?
options: A state is bound by every treaty in force, whether or not it has agreed to be bound
A state has supreme authority over its own territory and people, free from outside interference
A state must follow every resolution of the UN General Assembly once it has joined the United Nations
A state may use armed force against any neighbour that threatens its trade or economy
questions.explanation: Sovereignty gives each state supreme authority within its borders and the right to be free from interference by other states. General Assembly resolutions are recommendations rather than binding orders, and a state is bound only by the treaties it has consented to.

questions.stem: A government is accused of mass atrocities against a minority group inside its borders. It refuses entry to UN investigators, citing Article 2(7) of the UN Charter. Why does this make enforcing international law difficult?
options: The Charter requires investigators to obtain a warrant from the International Court of Justice before they can enter any country
The Charter protects matters within a state's domestic jurisdiction, so outside action generally needs the state's consent or Security Council enforcement
Article 2(7) gives every state a veto over any Security Council resolution about events taking place on its own territory
Article 2(7) means that international law applies only to wars fought between two or more states, never to events inside one state
questions.explanation: Article 2(7) bars the UN from intervening in matters essentially within a state's domestic jurisdiction, although it does not limit Chapter VII enforcement measures. Only the five permanent members hold a veto, and international law, including human rights law and the law of non-international armed conflict, does apply inside a state.

questions.stem: Which is an example of an intrastate conflict?
options: A border war fought between the armies of two neighbouring countries
A military alliance acting together to defend a member state from attack
A trade dispute between two states heard by a World Trade Organization panel
A civil war between a government and an armed rebel group within one country
questions.explanation: An intrastate conflict takes place within a single state, such as a civil war between a government and armed groups. A border war between two countries is an interstate conflict, and a trade dispute heard by a panel is not an armed conflict at all.

questions.stem: Which list best describes common causes of armed conflict?
options: Disputes over territory and resources, ethnic or religious tension, and competition for political power
The signing of peace treaties, membership of the United Nations and the growth of trade links between states
The work of peacekeepers, the ratification of human rights treaties and the holding of free elections
The presence of international NGOs, foreign aid programs and the activity of independent media
questions.explanation: Conflicts commonly arise from disputes over land and resources, ethnic, religious or ideological tension, and struggles for political control. Treaties, trade, aid and elections are generally ways of preventing conflict rather than causes of it.

questions.stem: Article 2(4) of the UN Charter requires member states to:
options: refrain from the threat or use of force against the territorial integrity or political independence of any state
contribute troops to any peacekeeping operation that the General Assembly or Secretary-General asks them to send
settle every dispute with another state by taking it to the International Court of Justice first
ratify the Geneva Conventions and the Rome Statute within one year of joining the United Nations
questions.explanation: Article 2(4) is the Charter's general prohibition on the threat or use of force in international relations. States are not obliged to send troops when asked, and they may choose among peaceful means of settlement rather than having to go to the ICJ.

questions.stem: Under the UN Charter, what are the two recognised exceptions to the prohibition on the use of force?
options: Self-defence against an armed attack under Article 51, and force authorised by the Security Council under Chapter VII
Force approved by a two-thirds majority of the General Assembly, and force used to collect unpaid international debts
Force used by a permanent member of the Security Council, and force used to change another state's government
Force approved by a regional organisation, and force used to protect a state's own trade routes and economic interests
questions.explanation: The Charter allows force in individual or collective self-defence if an armed attack occurs, and force authorised by the Security Council acting under Chapter VII. Being a permanent member gives no special right to use force, and the General Assembly cannot authorise enforcement action as the Council can.

questions.stem: How does Chapter VI of the UN Charter differ from Chapter VII?
options: Chapter VI covers conflicts between states, while Chapter VII covers human rights abuses within a single member state
Chapter VI deals with the peaceful settlement of disputes, while Chapter VII allows enforcement action for threats to the peace
Chapter VI sets out the powers of the General Assembly, while Chapter VII sets out the powers of the International Court of Justice
Chapter VI allows the use of armed force by member states, while Chapter VII only allows economic sanctions against states
questions.explanation: Chapter VI lists peaceful means such as negotiation, mediation, arbitration and judicial settlement. Chapter VII lets the Security Council determine a threat to the peace and take binding measures, from sanctions under Article 41 to armed force under Article 42.

questions.stem: The four Geneva Conventions of 1949 are the core treaties of:
options: international refugee law, defining who is a refugee and setting out the rights of asylum seekers in host states
international criminal law, establishing the permanent court that tries individuals for genocide
international humanitarian law, protecting people who are not or no longer taking part in hostilities
international trade law, setting the rules for tariffs and trade between states in times of peace
questions.explanation: The Geneva Conventions protect wounded and sick soldiers, shipwrecked sailors, prisoners of war and civilians during armed conflict. Refugee law rests on the 1951 Refugee Convention, and the permanent criminal court was created by the Rome Statute.

questions.stem: Why was the Rome Statute a significant development for collective security?
options: It banned the testing of nuclear weapons and created an international agency to inspect nuclear facilities around the world
It replaced the Geneva Conventions with a single treaty covering the conduct of all armed conflict
It created a permanent court able to hold individuals criminally responsible for the most serious international crimes
It created the Security Council and gave its five permanent members the power to veto any resolution
questions.explanation: The Rome Statute, adopted in 1998 and in force from 2002, created the International Criminal Court to try individuals for genocide, crimes against humanity, war crimes and aggression. The Security Council was created by the UN Charter in 1945, and the Geneva Conventions remain in force alongside the statute.

questions.stem: Which statement best describes the role of the International Committee of the Red Cross in armed conflict?
options: It is a UN court that tries military commanders and political leaders accused of breaching the Geneva Conventions
It is a military alliance that sends armed forces to protect civilians when a state cannot do so
It is an agency of the Security Council that decides when sanctions should be imposed on a state
It is a neutral humanitarian body that visits detainees, helps victims and promotes respect for humanitarian law
questions.explanation: The ICRC is an independent, neutral organisation with a special mandate under the Geneva Conventions to protect and assist victims of armed conflict. It has no judicial or military role; trials are for courts such as the ICC, and sanctions are decided by the Security Council.

questions.stem: Footage of attacks on civilians spreads widely online and governments face pressure to respond. Which is the best evaluation of the media's role in conflict?
options: It is the most effective legal response to conflict because media reports are binding evidence in international courts
It has replaced the need for NGOs, because media coverage alone now ensures states comply with humanitarian law
It weakens collective security in every case, because publicity always prolongs conflicts rather than ending them
It can raise awareness and pressure states to act, but coverage can be selective, inaccurate or used for propaganda
questions.explanation: Media coverage can expose abuses and build pressure for action, but it is uneven, can be manipulated and may spread misinformation. Reports are not automatically accepted as evidence, and they work alongside NGOs rather than replacing them.

questions.stem: How many members does the UN Security Council have?
options: 15, of which ten are permanent members
193, one for each UN member state
15, of which five are permanent members
10, of which five are permanent members
questions.explanation: The Security Council has five permanent members (China, France, Russia, the United Kingdom and the United States) and ten non-permanent members elected by the General Assembly for two-year terms. All 193 member states sit in the General Assembly, not the Council.

questions.stem: A draft Security Council resolution receives 13 votes in favour, one abstention and one vote against from a permanent member. What is the result?
options: The resolution fails, because a negative vote by a permanent member is a veto
The resolution passes, because it received more than nine votes in favour
The resolution passes, but it binds only the members that voted in favour
The resolution is sent to the General Assembly, which then decides it by vote
questions.explanation: A substantive Security Council decision needs nine votes in favour and no negative vote from any of the five permanent members. One permanent member voting against is a veto, however many others vote yes; an abstention, by contrast, is not treated as a veto.

questions.stem: The Security Council is deadlocked by a veto while a conflict threatens international peace. Under the Uniting for Peace resolution of 1950, the General Assembly may:
options: remove the vetoing state from the Security Council for a period of time
refer the permanent member that used the veto to the International Court
consider the matter and recommend collective measures to member states
override the veto by a two-thirds majority and issue a binding decision
questions.explanation: Resolution 377(V) allows the General Assembly to meet and make recommendations when the Council fails to act because of a lack of unanimity among the permanent members. The Assembly's recommendations are not binding, and it has no power to override a veto or remove a permanent member.

questions.stem: Which statement correctly describes the legal effect of decisions of the UN General Assembly and the Security Council?
options: General Assembly resolutions bind all member states, while Security Council decisions are recommendations to the members
Both bodies make binding decisions, but only for member states that voted in favour of the particular resolution
Neither body can make binding decisions, because only treaties ratified by each state can bind member states
Security Council decisions under Chapter VII bind all member states, while General Assembly resolutions are generally recommendations
questions.explanation: Under Article 25, members agree to carry out Security Council decisions, and Chapter VII decisions are binding on all. General Assembly resolutions on matters such as peace and security are recommendations, although they carry moral and political weight.

questions.stem: Which is an example of a regional intergovernmental organisation that promotes cooperation in Australia's region?
options: Amnesty International
The International Criminal Court
Medecins Sans Frontieres
The Pacific Islands Forum
questions.explanation: The Pacific Islands Forum is an intergovernmental organisation of states in the Pacific, including Australia and New Zealand. Amnesty International and Medecins Sans Frontieres are non-government organisations, and the ICC is an international court.

questions.stem: Under international humanitarian law, which obligation binds a non-state armed group fighting a government in a civil war?
options: Only the obligations in treaties the armed group has signed with the UN, which are enforced by the General Assembly
Common Article 3 of the Geneva Conventions, which requires humane treatment of people not taking part in hostilities
None, because only states can sign the Geneva Conventions, so armed groups are free of all humanitarian law obligations
The prohibition in Article 2(4) of the UN Charter, which binds armed groups exactly as it binds UN member states
questions.explanation: Common Article 3 applies to armed conflicts not of an international character and binds each party to the conflict, including non-state armed groups. Armed groups do not sign treaties, but they are still bound by these rules and their members can be prosecuted for war crimes.

questions.stem: Why do states provide mutual aid and assistance, such as disaster relief and development aid, to other states?
options: Aid gives the donor state legal control over the receiving state's laws, courts and budget for a fixed period of years
Aid is the only lawful way a state may respond to a breach of international law by another state
It builds stability and cooperative relationships, which reduces the conditions that can lead to conflict
The UN Charter requires every member to give a fixed share of its income to the states that request it
questions.explanation: Mutual aid strengthens relationships and helps address poverty and instability, which are common drivers of conflict. There is no Charter rule fixing aid amounts, and giving aid confers no legal control over another sovereign state.

questions.stem: In 1999 Australia led INTERFET, a multinational force sent to East Timor. What was the legal basis for the force?
options: A General Assembly resolution, which ordered Australia to occupy East Timor until independence
An ICJ judgment, which ordered Indonesia to hand East Timor over to Australian military control
The ANZUS Treaty, which allows Australia to send troops into any neighbouring state without that state's consent
Security Council Resolution 1264, which authorised it under Chapter VII to restore peace and security
questions.explanation: INTERFET was authorised by the Security Council in Resolution 1264 in September 1999 and handed over to the UN peacekeeping force of UNTAET in February 2000. The General Assembly cannot order enforcement action, and no ICJ judgment created the force.

questions.stem: The Regional Assistance Mission to Solomon Islands (RAMSI) ran from 2003 to 2017. Which statement best describes it?
options: A regional mission led by Australia at the Solomon Islands government's request, under the Pacific Islands Forum's Biketawa Declaration
A UN peacekeeping operation authorised by the Security Council under Chapter VII after the Solomon Islands invaded a neighbouring state
A NATO mission sent to the Solomon Islands under Article 5 of the North Atlantic Treaty to defend Australia from an armed attack
An ICC investigation led by Australian police into war crimes committed during a conflict between the Solomon Islands and Fiji
questions.explanation: RAMSI was invited by the Solomon Islands government to restore law and order and rebuild institutions, and it was mobilised under the Forum's 2000 Biketawa Declaration. It was a regional, consent-based mission, not a Chapter VII UN operation or a NATO deployment.

questions.stem: Which development best illustrates the changing nature of war since 1945?
options: Wars are now fought only between the permanent members of the Security Council using conventional armies
The Geneva Conventions have been replaced, so modern conflicts are no longer governed by any legal rules
Armed conflicts now end only when the International Court of Justice orders the parties to stop fighting
Most armed conflicts are now within states and involve non-state armed groups rather than wars between states
questions.explanation: Since 1945 the typical conflict has shifted from interstate war to intrastate conflict involving rebels, militias and terrorist groups, along with new technologies such as drones and cyber operations. The Geneva Conventions remain in force and apply to modern conflicts.

questions.stem: A state's power grid is disabled by a cyber operation launched from another state. Why does this challenge existing international law?
options: It can be hard to identify who carried out the attack and to decide whether it amounts to a use of force or an armed attack
Cyber operations are expressly permitted by the UN Charter, so the victim state has no lawful response available to it
International law applies only to weapons that existed in 1945, so cyber operations fall outside all legal rules
Only the International Criminal Court may decide whether a cyber operation has occurred, and it has refused to do so
questions.explanation: Attribution is difficult in cyberspace, and it is debated when a cyber operation crosses the threshold of a use of force or an armed attack that triggers self-defence. States generally accept that existing international law applies to cyber operations, but its application is unsettled.

questions.stem: Under international humanitarian law, the principle of distinction requires parties to a conflict to:
options: distinguish between states that have ratified the Geneva Conventions and states that have refused to ratify them
distinguish between soldiers of different ranks when deciding how prisoners of war are treated
distinguish between combatants and civilians, and between military objectives and civilian objects
distinguish between wars of aggression and wars of self-defence before deciding which rules apply
questions.explanation: Distinction means attacks may be directed only at combatants and military objectives, never at civilians or civilian objects. Humanitarian law applies equally to all parties, whichever side started the war.

questions.stem: A commander plans an attack on a legitimate military target, knowing it will cause civilian deaths far greater than the military advantage gained. Which principle of humanitarian law does the attack breach?
options: Proportionality
Military necessity
Sovereign equality
Self-determination
questions.explanation: Proportionality prohibits attacks expected to cause incidental civilian harm that would be excessive compared with the concrete and direct military advantage anticipated. Military necessity permits only the force needed to achieve a legitimate military aim and does not justify excessive civilian harm.

questions.stem: Which statement best describes the principle of humanity in international humanitarian law?
options: It requires armed forces to stop fighting whenever an NGO asks them to allow humanitarian aid workers into a conflict area
It forbids inflicting suffering, injury or destruction that is not necessary to achieve a legitimate military purpose
It requires every state to accept refugees from any conflict, whatever the number of refugees seeking protection
It allows a state to use any weapon it chooses, provided it has declared war on the other state beforehand
questions.explanation: The principle of humanity limits the means and methods of warfare by prohibiting unnecessary suffering. Refugee protection comes from refugee law, and humanitarian law restricts weapons whether or not war has been declared.

questions.stem: How did the Security Council respond to atrocities in the former Yugoslavia and in Rwanda in the 1990s?
options: It passed General Assembly resolutions ordering national courts in each state to hold trials
It created ad hoc international criminal tribunals, the ICTY and the ICTR, to try individuals responsible
It asked the International Court of Justice to try the individual commanders accused of genocide
It referred both situations to the International Criminal Court, which was then already operating
questions.explanation: Acting under Chapter VII, the Council set up the ICTY in 1993 and the ICTR in 1994. The ICC did not begin operating until 2002, and the ICJ hears disputes between states rather than criminal trials of individuals.

questions.stem: Which statement correctly distinguishes the International Court of Justice from the International Criminal Court?
options: The ICJ hears appeals from the ICC, which sits in New York as the trial court for the United Nations
The ICJ hears cases only about human rights, while the ICC hears cases only about disputed borders
The ICJ settles legal disputes between states, while the ICC tries individuals for the most serious international crimes
The ICJ tries individuals for war crimes, while the ICC gives advisory opinions to the UN General Assembly
questions.explanation: The ICJ is the principal judicial organ of the UN and decides disputes between consenting states and gives advisory opinions. The ICC, created by the Rome Statute, prosecutes individuals for genocide, crimes against humanity, war crimes and aggression. Both sit in The Hague and neither hears appeals from the other.

questions.stem: Under the principle of complementarity, when may the International Criminal Court hear a case?
options: Whenever a state party asks it to, even if national courts are already conducting a genuine trial
Only after the International Court of Justice has found the state responsible for the crime
Only when the accused person agrees to be tried in The Hague rather than in a national court
When national courts are unwilling or unable genuinely to investigate or prosecute the crime
questions.explanation: The ICC is a court of last resort: national courts have the first responsibility to prosecute, and the ICC acts only when a state is unwilling or unable to do so genuinely. Australia's International Criminal Court Act 2002 helps it meet this responsibility through its own courts.

questions.stem: Targeted sanctions such as asset freezes and travel bans are often preferred to broad trade embargoes. Why?
options: They are binding on every state in the world, whereas trade embargoes bind only the state that imposes them
They need no Security Council resolution, whereas every trade embargo must be approved by the ICJ
They guarantee that the targeted state will comply quickly, whereas trade embargoes never change behaviour
They aim at the leaders and entities responsible while limiting harm to the general civilian population
questions.explanation: Broad embargoes can cause serious hardship to ordinary people, so targeted measures focus on specific individuals, groups and companies. Whether sanctions bind all states depends on how they are imposed, and no form of sanction guarantees compliance.

questions.stem: Under the 1951 Refugee Convention, a refugee is a person outside their country who has a well-founded fear of persecution because of:
options: race, religion, nationality, membership of a particular social group or political opinion
poverty, unemployment, natural disaster, climate change or a lack of basic health services
a criminal conviction, a pending trial, a civil debt or a dispute with an employer at home
any armed conflict in their region, whether or not they personally face a risk of harm
questions.explanation: The Convention definition rests on persecution for one of five grounds. People fleeing poverty or disaster are not refugees under this definition, although they may be protected in other ways.

questions.stem: What did the 1967 Protocol Relating to the Status of Refugees change?
options: It extended refugee status to every person displaced within their own country by armed conflict
It created the UN High Commissioner for Refugees and gave it power to grant asylum on behalf of states
It allowed states to return refugees to danger if they arrived without a visa or travel documents
It removed the time and geographic limits so the Convention applies to refugees from any event, anywhere
questions.explanation: The 1951 Convention was limited to events before 1 January 1951, and states could limit it to Europe; the 1967 Protocol removed these limits. UNHCR was established by the General Assembly in 1950, and the Convention forbids returning refugees to persecution.

questions.stem: Why are internally displaced persons (IDPs) more difficult to protect under international law than refugees?
options: They have not crossed an international border, so they remain under the protection of their own state
They are excluded from the Geneva Conventions, so humanitarian law gives them no protection
They are treated as combatants, so they may be lawfully targeted during an armed conflict
They have committed crimes, so they lose all rights under international human rights law
questions.explanation: The Refugee Convention protects people outside their own country, so IDPs depend on their own government, which may be the cause of their displacement. The non-binding Guiding Principles on Internal Displacement of 1998 set out standards, and IDPs keep their protection as civilians under humanitarian law.

questions.stem: Under the Responsibility to Protect (R2P), as agreed at the 2005 World Summit, a state's primary responsibility is to protect its population from:
options: foreign trade barriers, currency crises and economic sanctions
terrorism, organised crime, cyber attacks and drug trafficking
genocide, war crimes, ethnic cleansing and crimes against humanity
poverty, unemployment, disease and the effects of climate change
questions.explanation: Paragraphs 138 and 139 of the 2005 World Summit Outcome limit R2P to four mass atrocity crimes. It does not extend to poverty, economic problems or crime generally.

questions.stem: In 2011 the Security Council adopted Resolution 1973 on Libya. How does it relate to the third pillar of R2P?
options: It recognised Libya's sovereign right to deal with rebels as it chose, applying the pillar of non-intervention in states
It authorised all necessary measures to protect civilians, as collective action when a state manifestly fails to protect its people
It ordered Libya to request help from neighbouring states, applying the pillar that requires states to accept regional assistance
It referred Libya to the ICJ, applying the pillar that makes the court responsible for preventing mass atrocity crimes
questions.explanation: Pillar three provides for timely and decisive collective action through the Security Council when a state manifestly fails to protect its population. Resolution 1973, adopted under Chapter VII with ten votes and five abstentions, authorised measures including a no-fly zone to protect civilians.

questions.stem: How does peacebuilding differ from peacekeeping?
options: Peacebuilding is carried out only by NGOs, while peacekeeping is carried out only by the permanent Security Council members
Peacebuilding begins before any conflict starts, while peacekeeping begins only after the ICC has issued arrest warrants
Peacebuilding addresses the root causes of conflict to build lasting peace, while peacekeeping helps maintain a ceasefire
Peacebuilding uses armed force to end a war, while peacekeeping uses only diplomacy between leaders before fighting begins
questions.explanation: Peacekeeping operations help keep the peace where fighting has stopped, while peacebuilding strengthens institutions, the rule of law and the economy so that conflict does not return. Both involve many actors, including states, the UN and NGOs.

questions.stem: Which three principles traditionally guide UN peacekeeping operations?
options: Consent of the parties, impartiality, and no use of force except in self-defence and defence of the mandate
Consent of the General Assembly, neutrality of the ICJ, and use of force against any party that breaks the law
Consent of the Secretary-General, support for the stronger party, and full use of force to end the conflict
Consent of the ICC, support for the government, and use of force to punish those accused of war crimes
questions.explanation: Peacekeeping relies on the consent of the main parties, impartiality between them, and the non-use of force except in self-defence and defence of the mandate. Impartiality does not mean supporting the stronger side, and peacekeepers do not enforce criminal punishment.

questions.stem: Which is an example of diplomacy being used to maintain relationships between states?
options: Two states negotiate a maritime boundary treaty through their foreign ministers
One state freezes the assets of another state's leaders in its banks
One state sends troops across a border to seize disputed territory
One state's court tries a foreign soldier for a war crime overseas
questions.explanation: Diplomacy is the conduct of relations between states through negotiation and dialogue, such as treaty negotiations. Freezing assets is a sanction, sending troops is a use of force, and a war crimes trial is a judicial response.

questions.stem: What are the three pillars of the Treaty on the Non-Proliferation of Nuclear Weapons (NPT)?
options: Non-proliferation, disarmament and the peaceful use of nuclear energy
Deterrence, retaliation and the expansion of nuclear arsenals
Sanctions, prosecution and the use of force against new nuclear states
Testing, stockpiling and the sharing of weapons among allied states
questions.explanation: The NPT, opened for signature in 1968 and in force from 1970, aims to stop the spread of nuclear weapons, pursue disarmament and support peaceful nuclear energy under IAEA safeguards. It does not authorise force against states that acquire weapons.

questions.stem: Which statement correctly compares two treaties on weapons of mass destruction?
options: The Biological Weapons Convention allows stockpiles for defence, while the Chemical Weapons Convention allows their use in self-defence
The Chemical Weapons Convention applies only to the five nuclear-weapon states, while the Biological Weapons Convention applies to all
The Biological Weapons Convention created the IAEA, while the Chemical Weapons Convention created the International Criminal Court
The Chemical Weapons Convention has a verification body, the OPCW, while the Biological Weapons Convention has no equivalent body
questions.explanation: The Chemical Weapons Convention, in force from 1997, is monitored by the Organisation for the Prohibition of Chemical Weapons, which inspects facilities and verifies destruction. The Biological Weapons Convention of 1972 lacks a comparable verification body, which is often seen as its main weakness.

questions.stem: The Treaty on the Prohibition of Nuclear Weapons entered into force in 2021. Why is its impact on nuclear disarmament limited?
options: It was adopted by the Security Council, so any permanent member can veto its operation
It is a General Assembly resolution, so it has no legal force for any state that votes
It applies only to nuclear testing at sea and does not cover the possession of weapons
A treaty binds only states that consent, so nuclear-armed states that stay out are not bound
questions.explanation: Under the principle of state consent, a treaty binds only its parties, so a nuclear-armed state that does not join is not bound by its ban. The treaty is a binding instrument that prohibits developing, possessing and using nuclear weapons, but only for the states that ratify it.
